title: Diagnosis of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis using liver stiffness measurement: comparison between M and XL probe of FibroScan®.
text_summary: 本文围绕“Diagnosis of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis using liver stiffness measurement: comparison between M and XL probe of FibroScan®.”开展研究，具体研究方法、结果和结论见论文正文。

Research Article

Diagnosis of liver ﬁbrosis and cirrhosis using liver
stiffness measurement: Comparison between M and XL probe
of FibroScanÒ
Victor de Lédinghen1,2,⇑, Vincent Wai-Sun Wong3,4, Julien Vergniol1, Grace Lai-Hung Wong3,4,
Juliette Foucher1, Shirley Ho-Ting Chu3,4, Brigitte Le Bail2,5, Paul Cheung-Lung Choi6,
Faiza Chermak1, Karen Kar-Lum Yiu3,4, Wassil Merrouche1, Henry Lik-Yuen Chan3,4
1

Centre d’Investigation de la Fibrose Hépatique, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire (CHU) de Bordeaux, Hôpital Haut-Lévêque,
France; 2Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale U1053, Université Bordeaux Segalen, Bordeaux,
France; 3Institute of Digestive Disease, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China; 4Department of Medicine and Therapeutics,
The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China; 5Service d’Anatomie Pathologique, CHU de Bordeaux,
Hôpital Pellegrin, France; 6Department of Anatomical and Cellular Pathology, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China

Background & Aims: Unreliable results of liver stiffness measurement are obtained in 16% of cases and are independently
associated with body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 kg/m2.
A new FibroScanÒ probe (XL probe) was designed speciﬁcally
for obese patients. The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of liver stiffness measurement using M and XL probes of
FibroscanÒ for the diagnosis of ﬁbrosis and cirrhosis in a large
cohort of patients.
Methods: Consecutive patients undergoing liver biopsies for
chronic liver disease were prospectively recruited. Liver stiffness
measurement was performed within 1 week before liver biopsy
using both M and XL probes of FibroScanÒ.
Results: A total of 286 patients were evaluated. A reliable liver
stiffness measurement using M probe was obtained in 79.7% of
cases. In the other 21.3%, liver stiffness measurement using XL
probe was obtained in 56.9% of patients. A strong correlation
was found between M and XL values, regardless of BMI. In all
groups, median liver stiffness measurement using the XL probe
was signiﬁcantly lower than liver stiffness measurement using
the M probe. By multivariate analysis, unsuccessful liver stiffness
examination with M probe was independently associated with
age >50 years and BMI >30 kg/m2. By univariate analysis, only
BMI >30 kg/m2 was associated with unsuccessful liver stiffness
measurement with XL probe. No signiﬁcant difference was
observed between the M and XL probes for the diagnosis of liver
ﬁbrosis.

Keywords: Cirrhosis; Biopsy; ROC curve; Sensitivity and speciﬁcity; NAFLD;
NASH; Hepatitis C; Liver ﬁbrosis.

Conclusions: Liver stiffness measurement with either M or XL
probe is possible in 91.2% of patients with comparable diagnostic
accuracy. In clinical practice, the M probe could be used as ﬁrst
step for liver stiffness measurement. In case of no valid shot or
unreliable measurement, the XL probe could be used. This result
could be useful for the assessment of liver ﬁbrosis in NAFLD and/
or obese patients.

Introduction
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is one of the most common chronic liver diseases worldwide [1,2]. It is strongly associated with metabolic syndrome and obesity, and may progress to
cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma [3]. The prognosis
depends heavily on histological severity. Although patients with
simple steatosis have excellent prognosis, those with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis tend to progress and have hepatic complications [4]. NAFLD is associated with the metabolic syndrome such
as insulin resistance, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity [5].
Liver stiffness measurement by Fibroscan is a noninvasive
method for the diagnosis of liver ﬁbrosis. It has a high degree of
accuracy and reproducibility in predicting bridging ﬁbrosis and
cirrhosis in patients with chronic liver diseases, especially NAFLD
[6–10]. In a recent study, we found that in 246 NAFLD patients the
area under the receiver-operating characteristics curve (AUROC)
of liver stiffness measurement for F3 or higher and F4 disease
was 0.93 and 0.95, respectively. However, in this study, 10.2% of
patients were excluded because of failure to obtain 10 valid liver
stiffness measurement acquisitions, especially because of an elevated body mass index (BMI). It is well-known that liver stiffness
measurement failure occurs in around 3% of all examinations, and
is independently associated with BMI greater than 30 kg/m2 in
both Caucasian and Chinese people [11,12]. Thus, between 1980
and 2008, mean BMI increased worldwide by 0.4 kg/m2 per

Journal of Hepatology 2012 vol. 56 j 833–839


Research Article
decade [13]. In 2008, an estimated 1.46 billion adults (1.41–
1.51 billion) worldwide had a BMI of 25 kg/m2 or greater; among
them, 205 million men (193–217 million) and 297 million women
(280–315 million) were obese [13].
To cater for such a special need, a new Fibroscan probe, named
the XL probe, was designed speciﬁcally for obese patients. This
new probe contains a lower frequency and a more sensitive ultrasonic transducer, a deeper focal length, a larger vibration amplitude and a higher depth of measurements below the skin surface
[14]. This new probe was evaluated in 99 obese patients (BMI
41 kg/m2, range: 30–64 kg/m2). Ten valid measurements were
obtained in 76% of cases using the XL probe, and 45% of cases
using the M probe (p <0.001). However, this study did not have
a histological correlation. A more recent study evaluated the performance of this new probe for the diagnosis of liver ﬁbrosis in 50
patients with NAFLD. All patients had liver stiffness measurement with the standard probe (M probe) and the new XL probe,
and the results were compared with liver histology. The diagnostic accuracy expressed as the area under the ROC curve for liver
stiffness measurement with the M probe and the XL probe was
0.80 and 0.82 for the diagnosis of signiﬁcant ﬁbrosis, and 0.91
and 0.95 for the diagnosis of cirrhosis, respectively. Eighty-three
percent of the patients who could not be measured with the M
probe could be measured using the XL probe [15].
The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of liver
stiffness measurement using M and XL probes of FibroscanÒ for
the diagnosis of ﬁbrosis and cirrhosis in a large cohort of patients.
We also aimed at identifying factors associated with no valid or
unreliable measurements using M or XL probe.

Patients and methods
Consecutive patients undergoing liver biopsies at the Prince of Wales Hospital,
Hong Kong and the University Hospital of Pessac, France were prospectively
recruited. We included patients aged 18 years or above who underwent a liver
biopsy for chronic liver disease. Aetiologies of chronic liver diseases were deﬁned
as usual. Men who consumed more than 30 g of alcohol per day and women who
consumed more than 20 g of alcohol per day were classiﬁed as alcoholic disease.
Patients with positive hepatitis B surface antigen or anti-hepatitis C virus antibody (and positive HCV RNA) were classiﬁed as viral hepatitis. All patients gave
written informed consent.
Clinical assessment
Comprehensive clinical assessment was performed. Co-morbid illness was
recorded with a standard questionnaire. Anthropometric tests included body
weight, body height, and waist circumference measurements. Body mass index
(BMI) was calculated as weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. Waist circumference was measured at a level midway between the lower rib margin and the
iliac crest with the tape all around the body in the horizontal position. Metabolic
syndrome was deﬁned as follow: waist circumference >94 cm for male and 80 cm
for female, anti-hypertensive treatment or blood pressure P130/85 mmHg, type
1 or type 2 diabetes, triglycerides >1.6 mmol/L, and HDL cholesterol <1.04 mmol/L
for male and <1.29 mmol/L for female [16].
On the day of liver biopsy, a fasting venous blood sample was taken for platelet count, bilirubin levels, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma glutamyl-transferase (GGT), total and high density
lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and triglycerides.
Histologic assessment
In this study, liver histology served as the gold standard for evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of transient elastography. Percutaneous liver biopsy was performed using the 16G Temno or Menghini needle. Liver biopsy specimens were
ﬁxed in formalin and embedded in parafﬁn. Liver histology was assessed by

834

experienced histopathologists (B.L.B., P.C.C.) who were blinded to the clinical
data. Liver specimens shorter than 11 mm in length were excluded. Histologic
scoring was performed according to the system reported by Kleiner et al. [17].
Grade of steatosis was deﬁned according to Kleiner et al.: 0 = steatosis <5%,
1 = steatosis 5–33%, 2 = steatosis >33–66%, 3 = steatosis >66%. Fibrosis was staged
from 0 to 4: stage 0 = absence of ﬁbrosis; stage 1 = perisinusoidal or portal; stage
2 = perisinusoidal and portal/periportal; stage 3 = septal or bridging ﬁbrosis; and
stage 4 = cirrhosis. In patients with viral hepatitis, METAVIR score was used
[18,19]. Fibrosis was staged on a 0–4 scale as follows: F0 = no ﬁbrosis; F1 = portal
ﬁbrosis without septa; F2 = portal ﬁbrosis and few septa; F3 = numerous septa
without cirrhosis; F4 = cirrhosis. Activity was graded as follows: A0 = none;
A1 = mild; A2 = moderate; A3 = severe. The length of each liver biopsy specimen
(in millimeters) was recorded.
Liver stiffness measurement
All consecutive patients undergoing liver biopsies had liver stiffness measurement by M and XL probes. Liver stiffness measurement was performed within
one week before liver biopsy (or the day of liver biopsy in France) using FibroScanÒ according to the instructions and training provided by the manufacturer.
Measurements were performed on the right lobe of the liver through intercostal
spaces, with the patient lying in dorsal decubitus with the right arm in maximal
abduction. Ten successful acquisitions were performed on each patient, ﬁrst
with M probe, then with XL probe. Both measurements were performed on
the same area. The median value represented the liver elastic modulus. For
comparison with liver biopsy, only cases with 10 successful acquisitions were
evaluated. The liver stiffness was expressed in kiloPascal (kPa). An IQR/liver
stiffness measurement >0.30 or less than 10 measurements deﬁned an unreliable result.
Statistical analysis
Statistical tests were performed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences
version 19.0. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation
or median (interquartile range [IQR]) as appropriate. Receiver-operating characteristics curves were constructed to assess the overall accuracy of liver stiffness
measurement. Quantitative variables between groups were compared by
unpaired t test or Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were compared
by Chi-squared test or Fisher’s exact test. The area under the receiver operating
characteristics curves of different non-invasive tests was compared by the Delong
test. Correlations between different variables were calculated by determination
coefﬁcient (r2). All statistical tests were two-sided. Signiﬁcance was taken as
p <0.05.

Results
From September 2009 to March 2011, 293 consecutive patients
with chronic liver disease underwent liver stiffness measurement
using M and XL probe of FibroScanÒ and liver biopsy. A total of
seven patients were excluded because of liver biopsy length less
than 11 mm. Therefore, 286 patients were included: 155 men,
median age 54.7 years, median BMI 25.9 kg/m2 (range: 16–
51 kg/m2). The clinical and biological characteristics of the 286
patients are listed in Table 1.
Feasibility of liver stiffness measurement
Feasibility of liver stiffness measurement with both probes is presented in Fig. 1. As indicated, reliable liver stiffness measurement
using M probe was obtained in 79.7% of cases. In the other 21.3%
of patients, liver stiffness measurement using XL probe was
obtained in 56.9% of patients. Therefore, liver stiffness measurement with either M or XL probe was possible in 91.2% of patients.
As indicated in Table 2, no valid shot was observed in 8.4% with M
probe and 1.7% with XL probe (p <0.001). All ﬁve patients with no
valid shot using XL probe had no valid shot using M probe. The

Factors associated with unsuccessful liver stiffness measurement
By univariate analysis, the factors associated with unsuccessful
liver stiffness measurement with M probe (no valid shot or unreliable measurement) were age >50 years (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI
1.4–5.9, p = 0.003), hypertension (OR 2.38, 95% CI 1.3–4.3,
p = 0.004), BMI >30 kg/m2 (OR 6.55, 95% CI 3.5–12.3, p <0.0001),
metabolic syndrome (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.3–4.1, p = 0.006), but
not gender, nor diabetes. By multivariate analysis, unsuccessful
liver stiffness examination was independently associated with
age >50 years (OR 3.53, 95% CI 1.6–8.0, p = 0.002), and BMI
>30 kg/m2 (OR 7.35, 95% CI 3.5–15.4, p <0.0001), but neither with
hypertension nor metabolic syndrome.
By univariate analysis, BMI >30 kg/m2 (OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.1–
4.2, p <0.02) was associated with unsuccessful liver stiffness measurement with the XL probe, but not age, gender, hypertension,
diabetes, or metabolic syndrome.
Steatosis and necroinﬂammation were not associated with
unsuccessful liver stiffness measurement with M or XL probe.
Accuracy of liver stiffness measurement
Using the M and XL probes, the median liver stiffness measurement of patients with F0, F1, F2, F3, and F4 disease was 5.8
[4.8–7.5] and 5.4 [4.5–6.7], 8.0 [6.2–9.6] and 7.3 [6.1–8.9], 9.9
[8.0–14.3] and 8.8 [6.1–11.9], 19.8 [12.9–48] and 17.3 [10.3–
38.8] kPa, respectively (p <0.0001 by ANOVA). Liver stiffness
measurement using the M and XL probes according to ﬁbrosis
stages is indicated in Fig. 3. No signiﬁcant difference was
observed between M and XL probe for the diagnosis of liver
ﬁbrosis.
No signiﬁcant correlation was found between the grade of steatosis and the liver stiffness measurement using M (r = 0.20) or
XL (r = 0.05) probe. Moreover, no signiﬁcant correlation was
found between necroinﬂammation and liver stiffness measurement using the M (r = 0.10) or XL (r = 0.10) probes.

836

To our knowledge, this study is the ﬁrst large multicentre study
to compare the new XL probe to the standard probe using liver
histology as a reference method. The results of the study show
that reliable measurement of liver ﬁbrosis is possible using the
XL probe with a diagnostic accuracy of 78% for the diagnosis of
signiﬁcant ﬁbrosis and 92% for the diagnosis of cirrhosis. Only
one previous study evaluated the performance of the XL probe
in NAFLD patients [15]. In this pilot study, reliable measurement
of liver ﬁbrosis was possible using the XL probe with a diagnostic
accuracy of 82% for the diagnosis of signiﬁcant ﬁbrosis and 91%
for the diagnosis of cirrhosis [15]. In this pilot study, 83% of
patients with measurement failure with the M probe could be
examined without failure with the XL probe. In this large study,
this prevalence was 91.3%.
In NAFLD patients, liver stiffness measurement is signiﬁcantly
correlated with age and BMI [20]. However, even when the liver
stiffness measurement is feasible, high BMI values negatively
affect the diagnostic reliability [21]. Therefore, in these patients,
an improved performance of transient elastography could be
obtained using XL probe.
In clinical practice, more than 9 out of 10 patients can have a
reliable liver stiffness measurement using either M or XL probe as
appropriate. The M probe could be used ﬁrst. In case of no valid
shot or in case of unreliable measurement, the XL probe could
be used. The higher unreliable liver stiffness measurement using
XL probe among patients with low BMI could indicate that, in
patients with BMI <25 kg/m2, only M probe should be used.
The median liver stiffness measured with the XL probe was
signiﬁcantly lower than that measured with the M probe (6.9
vs. 6.3 kPa, p <0.0001). The reason might be that non-hepatic tissue is involved in the measurement with the M probe in patients
with a skin-to-capsule distance greater than 25 mm. Recently,
Myers et al. also reported that in patients successfully measured
using both probes, liver stiffness tended to be lower using the XL
probe [22]. These differences were greatest at higher values of
liver stiffness and independent of liver disease etiology. These
ﬁndings presumably reﬂect the presence of adipose tissue in
the region of interest explored by the M probe in obese patients,
leading to overestimation of liver stiffness. In addition, the heterogeneity in hepatic ﬁbrosis (e.g. greater ﬁbrous tissue deposition
in the subcapsular region) and the differences in depth measurement between probes likely play a role in these ﬁndings. Therefore, the existing cut-offs deﬁned by using the M probe cannot
be used for the interpretation of liver stiffness measurements
using the XL probe. We did not evaluate AUROCs for each stage
of ﬁbrosis according to different groups of BMI. Indeed, not
enough patients per group were available. However, in patients
with BMI >30 kg/m2, especially NAFLD patients, the comparison
between M and XL probe for the diagnosis of severe ﬁbrosis
and cirrhosis is needed in future studies. As the failure rate of
M probe is high in patients with BMI >30 kg/m2, we could recommend the use of XL probe in all patients with BMI >30 kg/m2
(Table 3).
Our study has several limitations. Firstly, since different aetiologies were evaluated, we could not propose any cut-off value
for each stage of ﬁbrosis. Indeed, we know that each disease
has speciﬁc cut-offs for each stage of ﬁbrosis. Large prospective
studies with XL probe are needed to propose speciﬁc cut-off
values for each stage of ﬁbrosis, for each disease [6,8]. However,

the aim of our study was not to propose cut-offs for each stage of
ﬁbrosis but to compare the feasibility of the M and XL probes.
Secondly, liver biopsy was used as the gold standard, and liver
biopsies were assessed by two pathologists. Sampling bias could
not be excluded. However, liver biopsy is currently the only reference standard, and biopsies were assessed by experienced
pathologists. Moreover, only patients with liver biopsy
P10 mm were included. Thirdly, patients recruited at referral
centres likely had more advanced disease. Therefore, AUROCs
for the diagnosis of severe ﬁbrosis and cirrhosis could be higher
in our study. In this study, patients were not distributed equally
over stages F1–F4. Thus, we cannot exclude that this distribution
may have improved the predictive value of liver stiffness measurement. Unfortunately, the cohort was not large enough to

have a comparison stage by stage. Fourthly, the overall success
rate of FibroscanÒ was less than that of liver biopsy. When we
do liver biopsies, it is rare that no valid samples are obtained in
20% of cases. However, liver biopsy is an invasive procedure that
is not acceptable by all patients. Our current study clearly indicates that the use of XL probe can signiﬁcantly improve the success rate and valid measurements, particularly in obese patients.
Therefore, this is a signiﬁcant improvement from the current
standard of care, and can further reduce the burden of liver biopsies in clinical practice.
In summary, liver stiffness measurement using the XL probe
can be performed with a diagnostic accuracy comparable to that
of the standard probe (M probe), with the advantage of enabling
the examination of signiﬁcantly more patients. Therefore, in
